summary.countingMethod: 392 overlapping review groups: 248 complete glossary definitions with aliases/examples, 33 lesson units, 68 complete questions including every key/distractor, and 43 formula cards. These are not atomic facts. The recorded corrections count locations/fields, including reading-link corrections, rather than a count of distinct underlying misconceptions.

corrections.before: A quantity, such as a list's length or a counter, that decreases with every recursive call and can't decrease forever. Finding one proves that a recursion terminates.
corrections.after: A value ordered so there is no infinite descending chain. If every recursive call strictly decreases this measure, each invocation makes finitely many calls, and all other work terminates, recursion terminates too.

corrections.before: The argument n in countdown(n - 1) for n ≥ 0 is a well-founded measure.
corrections.after: For a countdown on nonnegative integers, return at zero and otherwise recur with n - 1; the measure cannot decrease forever.

corrections.before: A JavaScript error for a value outside its allowed range; engines also throw it when the call stack size is exceeded.
corrections.after: A JavaScript error type used for values outside an allowed range. The tested Node/V8 runtime also reports excessive recursion as RangeError; error types and messages for recursion exhaustion vary between engines.

corrections.before: https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html
corrections.after: https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/fundamental-objects.html

corrections.before: A fixed-size integer that fits in a processor register, such as a 64-bit Int in Haskell. Arithmetic on it is fast, but it can overflow.
corrections.after: A bounded integer type, commonly implemented using a machine word. Its range and overflow semantics depend on the language and implementation; Haskell Int is bounded while Integer is arbitrary precision.

corrections.before: Haskell's Int is 64 bits on 64-bit machines.
corrections.after: GHC normally uses a 64-bit Int on a 64-bit target; the Haskell Report guarantees only a minimum supported range.

corrections.before: On a 64-bit build of CPython each tuple slot is an 8-byte pointer.
corrections.after: Under a conventional eight-byte-pointer CPython ABI, each tuple reference slot occupies eight bytes; check the actual ABI.

corrections.before: Making a newly built object visible to other threads in a way that guarantees they see it fully initialised, such as through a lock, a volatile field or an atomic reference.
corrections.after: Making a newly built object visible to other threads with the required visibility and ordering guarantees. In Java, locks, volatile fields and atomic references can provide publication mechanisms; the correct rules depend on the language's memory model.

corrections.before: JavaScript's ... syntax, which copies the elements of an array or the properties of an object into a new array or object. It is the usual way to make an updated copy without mutating the original. The copy is shallow.
corrections.after: JavaScript's ... syntax expands an iterable into an array or argument list, or copies an object's own enumerable properties into an object literal. Object and array copies are shallow; nested objects remain shared.

corrections.before: A mutable variable used inside Haskell's ST monad. Its type ties it to one runST computation, so the mutation can't be observed from outside.
corrections.after: A mutable reference used inside Haskell's ST computation. Its state parameter and runST's rank-polymorphic type prevent a usable local mutable reference from escaping through safe typed code.

corrections.before: A React hook that manages state through a reducer function (state, action) → next state. React compares the next state with the previous one using Object.is, so a reducer must return a new object to signal a change.
corrections.after: A React hook that manages state with a reducer computing next state from state and an action. React can skip an update when Object.is says next and previous states are equal; changed object state needs a new identity.

corrections.before: The base of a number system: 10 for decimal, 2 for binary, 16 for hexadecimal. JavaScript's parseInt takes it as an optional second argument, from 2 to 36.
corrections.after: The base of a numeral system: 10 for decimal, 2 for binary and 16 for hexadecimal. JavaScript parseInt uses an optional radix after numeric conversion; 2 through 36 are explicit bases and zero requests base inference.

corrections.before: A JavaScript function, parseInt(string, radix), that parses a string as an integer in the given base. A radix of 0 or undefined means "work it out", usually decimal; 1 or values above 36 give NaN.
corrections.after: JavaScript parseInt converts its input to text and parses an integer prefix in a chosen radix. After radix conversion, zero requests base inference; values outside 2 through 36 produce NaN. Parsing can stop at the first invalid digit rather than rejecting the whole string.

corrections.after: https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/indexed-collections.html

corrections.before: (define (loop n) (if (= n 0) 'done (loop (- n 1)))) runs in constant space for any n.
corrections.after: A properly tail-recursive Scheme countdown need not retain one caller continuation per step; argument representation and other allocations still need their own space analysis.

corrections.before: A distributed data-processing engine. Its transformations (map, filter) only build a plan; nothing runs on the cluster until an action such as count or collect asks for a result.
corrections.after: A distributed data-processing engine. RDD map and filter defer their record transformations until an action demands results; source construction and driver setup can still inspect metadata or perform other work.

corrections.before: rdd.map(parse) is a transformation; it returns immediately.
corrections.after: rdd.map(parse) records a transformation without applying parse to the records yet.

corrections.before: The two rules a lawful map must obey: mapping the identity function changes nothing, and mapping f then g equals mapping their composition once. They guarantee map only transforms contents.
corrections.after: The two rules for a lawful mapping operation: mapping identity changes nothing, and mapping a composition equals composing the maps. For familiar container functors these express content transformation with preserved shape; functors need not be literal containers.

corrections.before: for { u <- findUser(1); t <- findTeam(u) } yield t chains two flatMaps.
corrections.after: Scala for { u <- findUser(1); t <- findTeam(u) } yield t uses an outer flatMap and a map for the final generator.

corrections.before: Python's a[i] is syntactic sugar for a.__getitem__(i).
corrections.after: Haskell do { x <- action; next x } translates to action >>= (\x -> next x).

corrections.before: A special value meaning "no object". Python calls it None, JavaScript has both null and undefined. Optional types make the possibility of absence explicit instead.
corrections.after: A distinguished value used to represent absence in some languages. Python has None; JavaScript distinguishes null and undefined. Optional types make possible absence explicit in the type.

corrections.before: https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html
corrections.after: https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/ecmascript-data-types-and-values.html

corrections.before: Syntax in JavaScript, Python, C#, Rust and other languages for writing asynchronous code as straight-line statements: await pauses an async function until a Promise, future or task completes and gives its result, letting other work run meanwhile.
corrections.after: Syntax for sequencing asynchronous operations using straight-line expressions. What await accepts, how a computation is driven, and whether already-completed work yields control depend on the language and runtime; JavaScript await accepts ordinary values as well as Promises.

corrections.before: A balanced tree of a million keys is about 20 levels deep.
corrections.after: A nearly complete binary tree with a million keys has about twenty node levels; other balance invariants permit different constant factors.

corrections.before: The maximum number of children a tree node has. A larger branching factor makes the tree shallower: 32 children per node give about log₃₂ n levels instead of log₂ n.
corrections.after: A bound on the number of children per tree node. In a densely occupied fixed-width trie, increasing it reduces the levels needed for a fixed capacity; actual depth also depends on occupancy and layout.

corrections.before: Sorting a million items takes on the order of 20 million comparisons.
corrections.after: A comparison-count model proportional to n log_2(n) gives about twenty million comparisons at a million items; actual algorithms and inputs differ.

corrections.before: A sequence of bits used as a compact set of flags. In a HAMT node, bit k is 1 when slot k has a child.
corrections.after: A sequence of bits used as compact flags. In a bitmap-indexed HAMT node, a set bit marks an occupied conceptual slot; concrete entries may represent a key/value pair or a child node.

corrections.before: A value holding the memory address of another value. Following a chain of pointers (pointer chasing) is slow when each load must wait for the one before.
corrections.after: A value used to refer to a storage location, often represented as a memory address. Following dependent pointers requires later addresses to wait for earlier loads; actual latency depends on layout, caches and the target.

corrections.before: https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/cheatsheet/
corrections.after: https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

corrections.before: Two different keys producing the same hash value. Hash structures need a fallback for it; HAMTs use special collision nodes.
corrections.after: Distinct keys producing the same hash value. Hash-based structures need a way to distinguish them; Clojure's HAMT includes explicit equal-hash collision nodes, while other implementations can use different fallbacks.

corrections.before: A thunk that stores its result after the first evaluation, so every version of a persistent structure that shares it pays for the work only once.
corrections.after: A delayed computation that stores its result after evaluation, allowing users of that same suspension to share the work. Persistent versions avoid repeated expensive work only if their design actually shares the relevant suspension; independently created thunks do not.

corrections.before: For a **balanced tree** (one whose branches all have roughly the same depth) of n keys, the path has logarithmic length.
corrections.after: For a **balanced tree** of n keys, a balance invariant bounds path length logarithmically; it need not put every leaf at nearly the same depth.

corrections.before: If two references point to the same object, nothing inside changed.
corrections.after: For deeply immutable values, two references to the same object refer to unchanged contents. Mutable objects can change while retaining identity.

corrections.before: Scala's `for` comprehensions and F#'s computation expressions do the same job.
corrections.after: Scala's `for` comprehensions express related map/flatMap sequencing. F# computation expressions use builder-defined operations and can express monadic sequencing as well as other abstractions.

corrections.before: a tail-recursive loop is *guaranteed* constant space.
corrections.after: a tail-call chain need not accumulate caller continuations. Other retained data and argument computation can still grow.

corrections.before: const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { todos: [] }).
corrections.after: const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { todos: [] }); changed object state should receive a new identity.

corrections.before: A structure, such as the list of all natural numbers, that is conceptually endless but usable under lazy evaluation because only the parts actually examined are ever built.
corrections.after: A conceptually endless structure whose demanded finite prefixes can be represented incrementally. Lazy consumers can use a productive infinite list, but a definition that never produces the next demanded constructor can still fail to yield a result.

corrections.before: https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/control-abstraction-objects.html
corrections.after: https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html

corrections.before: Big-O notation for a cost that grows with the logarithm of n, adding roughly a constant amount of work each time n doubles (or, for a 32-way trie, each time n grows 32-fold).
corrections.after: An asymptotic upper bound by a constant times the logarithm of an input-size parameter n, for sufficiently large n. The base changes constant factors; the bound does not assert an exact operation count.

corrections.before: A balanced tree of a million keys needs about 20 steps; of two million, about 21.
corrections.after: A nearly complete binary tree has about twenty node levels at a million keys and twenty-one at two million.

corrections.after: Each non-base invocation makes two recursive calls; the branches stop at different depths:

corrections.before: What does this print in a non-strict (sloppy mode) script?
corrections.after: What does this print in a JavaScript sloppy-mode script?
corrections.reason: Actual compiled rendering links bare non-strict to non-strict evaluation, the opposite language concept here; the precise sloppy-mode alias opens the JavaScript definition.

corrections.before: def naturals(): n = 1; while True: yield n; n += 1 generates 1, 2, 3, ... forever.
corrections.after: A Python generator can yield a counter starting at one, then increment it after each resumed yield to produce 1, 2, 3 and so on.
corrections.reason: The inherited semicolon-packed def/while sketch was not valid Python source. Replaced it with an accurate plain-language example; complete runnable lesson code is preserved.

gaps: The original module teaches practical monad patterns, not a full category-theory development or general proofs for partial/effectful programs.

Promise cancellation and scheduling, transformer stacks, streaming-library resource protocols, and library implementation internals are qualified introductory coverage rather than exhaustive implementations.
No production performance benchmark or universal memory threshold is claimed; vector allocation is an explicit pointer-payload model and collector costs depend on workload.

No arbitrary-program functor/monad proof, portable recursion threshold or production benchmark is claimed. The lazy ten-million fold remains a bounded incomplete execution; strict counterpart and finite forcing/law models pass.

Runtime comparison rows without executable fences are primary-source reviewed. Native displayed Python/Node/Haskell/Rust code and supplemental Java Optional cases were exercised with explicit local fixtures; no real external service is called.

fp-pure-functions.md: Distinguish unhashability from a hash that changes.
